'''Toshiko K. Mayeda''' (née Kuki) (1923–13 February 2004) was a Japanese American chemist who worked at the [[Enrico Fermi Institute]] in the [[University of Chicago]]. She worked on climate science and meteorites from 1958 to 2004.

== Early life and education ==
Toshiko Mayeda was born in [[Tacoma, Washington]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www-news.uchicago.edu/releases/04/040218.mayeda.shtml|title=Toshiko K. Mayeda, Chemist, 1923-2004|website=www-news.uchicago.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-08-05}}</ref> She grew up in [[Yokkaichi, Mie]], and [[Osaka]].<ref name=":0" /> When the United States entered [[World War II]] after the Japanese [[attack on Pearl Harbor]], she and her father Matsusaburo Kuki were sent to the [[Tule Lake Unit, World War II Valor in the Pacific National Monument|Tule Lake War Relocation Center]].<ref name=archives>{{cite web | title=Japanese American Internee Data File: Toshiko Kuki|url=https://aad.archives.gov/aad/record-detail.jsp?dt=3099&mtch=2&tf=F&q=Kuki&bc=&rpp=10&pg=1&rid=39303&rlst=39302,39303|publisher=[[National Archives and Records Administration]]| access-date=August 18, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://digitalassets.lib.berkeley.edu/jarda/ucb/text/reduced/cubanc6714_b265r20_0092.pdf|title=Social Welfare Appointment Notes|date=1943-09-20|website=Berkeley|access-date=2018-08-05}}</ref> Whilst there she met her future husband, Harry Mayeda.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://library.csus.edu/sites/default/files/JAAC_Finding_Aid.pdf|title=Japanese American Archival Collection|website=Sacramento State|access-date=2018-08-06}}</ref> After the war, she graduated with a bachelor's degree in chemistry from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1949.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://magazine.uchicago.edu/0406/alumni/deaths.shtml|title=The University of Chicago Magazine: June 2004|website=magazine.uchicago.edu|access-date=2018-08-05}}</ref>

== Research ==
Mayeda worked initially as a laboratory assistant to [[Harold Urey]] at the University of Chicago, where she was hired initially to wash glassware.<ref name="nature">{{cite journal|last=Van Tiggelen|first=Bridget|year=2019|title=The women behind the periodic table|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=565|pages=561|url=https://media.nature.com/original/magazine-assets/d41586-019-00287-7/d41586-019-00287-7.pdf}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2004/02/19/toshiko-k-mayeda-81/|title=Toshiko K. Mayeda, 81|work=tribunedigital-chicagotribune|access-date=2018-08-05|language=en}}</ref> They used [[mass spectrometry]] to measure [[Oxygen isotope ratio cycle|oxygen isotopes]] in the shells of marine [[Mollusca|molluscs]] which gave information on the prehistoric temperatures of ocean waters and hence [[Paleoclimatology|paleoclimates]].<ref name="Isotopes">{{cite book |doi=10.1142/9789811206290_0033 |chapter=Toshiko Mayeda and the Isotopes of Oxygen |title=Women in Their Element |year=2019 |last1=Shindell |first1=Matthew |pages=415–421 |isbn=978-981-12-0628-3|s2cid=201220619 }}</ref> Urey developed the field of [[cosmochemistry]] and with Mayeda studied primitive [[meteorite]]s, also by using [[oxygen isotope]] analysis.<ref>{{cite book |isbn=9780226662084 |last=Shindell |first=Matthew |title=The Life and Science of Harold C. Urey |date=2019 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |location=Chicago, Illinois|ref=Shindell}}</ref> Later, she worked with [[Cesare Emiliani]] on isotopic evaluation of the [[ice age]].<ref name="EMILIANI 1961 679">{{Cite journal|last1=Emiliani |first1=C. |last2=Mayeda |first2=T. |last3=Selli|first3=R.|date=1961|title=Paleotemperature Analysis of the Plio-Pleistocene Section at Le Castella, Calabria, Southern Italy|journal=Geological Society of America Bulletin|language=en|volume=72|issue=5|pages=679|doi=10.1130/0016-7606(1961)72[679:PAOTPS]2.0.CO;2|issn=0016-7606}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=The composition of matter : symposium honouring Johannes Geiss on the occasion of his 80th birthday|date=2007|publisher=Springer|others=Steiger, R. von (Rudolf), Gloeckler, G., Mason, G. M. (Glenn Marggraf), 1943-, Geiss, Johannes., International Space Science Institute.|isbn=9780387741840|location=New York|oclc=209984881}}</ref> When Urey retired from the university in 1958, Mayeda was persuaded to remain there by [[Robert N. Clayton]], and collaborate with him on applications of mass spectroscopy.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Clayton|first=Robert N.|date=May 2007|title=Isotopes: From Earth to the Solar System|journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences|language=en|volume=35|issue=1|pages=1–19|doi=10.1146/annurev.earth.35.092006.145059|issn=0084-6597|bibcode=2007AREPS..35....1C|doi-access=free}}</ref> She was described as an ''indomitable'' research assistant''.''<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Citation on the Award of the Leonard Medal of the Meteoritical Society to Dr. Robert N. Clayton|journal=Meteoritics|volume=17|issue=4|pages=171–174|doi=10.1111/j.1945-5100.1982.tb00090.x|year = 1982|last1 = Wood|first1 = John A.}}</ref><ref name="CWorld">{{cite journal |url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/culture/the-indomitable-toshiko-mayeda/4011147.article |title=The indomitable Toshiko Mayeda |last1=Shindell |first1=Matthew |date=March 2020 |journal=Chemistry World |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=36–37}}</ref>

Mayeda and Clayton's first research paper considered the use of [[Bromine pentafluoride]] to extract [[Isotopes of oxygen]] from rocks and minerals.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|date=1963-01-01|title=The use of bromine pentafluoride in the extraction of oxygen from oxides and silicates for isotopic analysis|journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta|language=en|volume=27|issue=1|pages=43–52|doi=10.1016/0016-7037(63)90071-1|issn=0016-7037|bibcode=1963GeCoA..27...43C|last1=Clayton|first1=Robert N.|last2=Mayeda|first2=Toshiko K.}}</ref> It remains their most cited work.<ref name=Isotopes /> From the 1970s until the late 1990s Mayeda and Clayton became famous for their use of oxygen isotopes to classify meteorites.<ref name=":2" /> They developed several tests that were used across the field of meteorite and lunar sample analysis.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.myscience.org/news/2018/robert_n_clayton_one_of_the_giants_of_cosmochemistry_1930_2017-2018-chicago|title=Robert N. Clayton, 'one of the giants' of cosmochemistry, 1930-2017|website=www.myscience.org|date=11 January 2018 |language=en|access-date=2018-08-05}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.elementsmagazine.org/archives/e14_2/e14_2_soc_MetSoc.pdf|title=In Memorian, Bob Clayton (1930–2017)|website=Elements Magazine|access-date=2018-08-06}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=1976-04-01|title=A classification of meteorites based on oxygen isotopes|journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters|language=en|volume=30|issue=1|pages=10–18|doi=10.1016/0012-821X(76)90003-0|issn=0012-821X|bibcode=1976E&PSL..30...10C|last1=Clayton|first1=Robert N.|last2=Onuma|first2=Naoki|last3=Mayeda|first3=Toshiko K.}}</ref> They studied variations in the abundances of the stable isotopes of oxygen, [[oxygen-16]], [[oxygen-17]] and [[oxygen-18]],<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ghcwDwAAQBAJ&q=asteroid+toshiko+mayeda&pg=PA89|title=Asteroids: Astronomical and Geological Bodies|last=Burbine|first=Thomas H.|date=2016-12-15|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9781316867396|pages=89|language=en}}</ref> and deduced differences in the formation temperatures of the meteorites.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1972-02-01|title=Oxygen isotope cosmothermometer|journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta|language=en|volume=36|issue=2|pages=169–188|doi=10.1016/0016-7037(72)90005-1|issn=0016-7037|bibcode=1972GeCoA..36..169O|last1=Onuma|first1=Naoki|last2=Clayton|first2=Robert N.|last3=Mayeda|first3=Toshiko K.}}</ref> They also worked on the mass spectroscopy and chemistry of the [[Allende meteorite]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal|date=1977-03-01|title=Distribution of the pre-solar component in Allende and other carbonaceous chondrites|journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters|language=en|volume=34|issue=2|pages=209–224|doi=10.1016/0012-821X(77)90005-X|issn=0012-821X|bibcode=1977E&PSL..34..209C|last1=Clayton|first1=R. N.|last2=Onuma|first2=N.|last3=Grossman|first3=L.|last4=Mayeda|first4=T. K.}}</ref> They published many scientific papers on the "oxygen thermometer" and analysed approximately 300 lunar samples that had been collected during [[NASA]]s [[Apollo Program]].<ref name=Isotopes/><ref name=CWorld />
In 1992, a new type of meteorite, the [[Brachinite]], was identified.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=E.|first1=Nehru, C.|last2=M.|first2=Prinz|last3=K.|first3=Weisberg, M.|last4=M.|first4=Ebihara|last5=N.|first5=Clayton, R.|last6=K.|first6=Mayeda, T.|date=July 1992|title=Brachinites: A New Primitive Achondrite Group|journal=Meteoritics|language=en|volume=27|issue=3|pages=267|issn=0026-1114|bibcode=1992Metic..27R.267N}}</ref> Clayton and Mayeda studied the [[Achondrite]] meteorites and showed that variations in the oxygen-17 isotope ratios within a planet are due to inhomogeneities in the [[Solar Nebula]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1996-06-01|title=Oxygen isotope studies of achondrites|journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta|language=en|volume=60|issue=11|pages=1999–2017|doi=10.1016/0016-7037(96)00074-9|issn=0016-7037|bibcode=1996GeCoA..60.1999C|last1=Clayton|first1=Robert N.|last2=Mayeda|first2=Toshiko K.}}</ref> They analysed [[Shergotty meteorite]]s, proposing that there could have been a water-rich atmosphere on [[Mars]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bouvier|first=A.|display-authors=etal |date=2009|title=Martian meteorite chronology and the evolution of the interior of Mars|journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters|volume=280|issue=1–4|pages=285–295|doi=10.1016/j.epsl.2009.01.042|bibcode=2009E&PSL.280..285B}}</ref> and studied the Bocaiuva meteorite, finding that the [[Eagle Station meteorite]] was formed due to impact heating.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Malvin|first1=Daniel J.|last2=Wasson|first2=John T.|last3=Clayton|first3=Robert N.|last4=Mayeda|first4=Toshiko K.|last5=Curvello|first5=Walter Silva|title=Bocaiuva-A Silicate-Inclusion Bearing Iron Meteorite Related to the Eagle-Station Pallasites|date=1985|journal=Meteoritics|volume=20|issue=2|pages=259–273|doi=10.1111/j.1945-5100.1985.tb00864.x|bibcode=1985Metic..20..259M |issn=0026-1114}}</ref>

In 2002 Mayeda was awarded the Society Merit Prize from the [[Geochemical Society of Japan]].<ref name=":1" /> In the same year, an asteroid was named after her.<ref name=":1" />  Mayeda's husband, Harry, died in 2003. Mayeda suffered from cancer and died on February 13, 2004.<ref name=":1" /> In 2008, the book ''Oxygen in the Solar System'' was dedicated to Clayton and Mayeda.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/solar-system-book-dedicated-robert-clayton-mr-oxygen|title=Solar system book dedicated to Robert Clayton, 'Mr. Oxygen'|website=University of Chicago News|date=22 May 2008 |language=en|access-date=2018-08-05}}</ref>
